title: External Fetal Heart Rate Monitoring (EFM)
summary: Applying and interpreting continuous external electronic fetal monitoring during labor.
equipment: Fetal monitor with tocodynamometer and ultrasound transducer
Nonreassuring FHR strip — call provider immediately
steps: Verify provider order. Explain procedure to patient.
Position patient in lateral or semi-Fowler position — avoid supine hypotension.
Apply gel to ultrasound transducer. Locate fetal heart rate using Doppler first.
Secure ultrasound transducer over the point of maximum intensity (PMI) with belt.
Position tocodynamometer (toco) at the fundus — secure with second belt.
Confirm baseline FHR (110–160 bpm is normal). Zero the toco. Start the strip.
Assess and document: baseline FHR, variability (moderate = reassuring), accelerations, decelerations, and contraction frequency/duration.
Category I strip: normal baseline, moderate variability, absent late/variable decelerations — continue monitoring.
Category II or III strip: notify provider immediately; reposition patient, administer O2 10L via NRB, increase IV fluids, discontinue oxytocin if running.
Perform Leopold maneuvers to confirm fetal position as needed.
Document strip interpretation every 15–30 minutes active labor, every 5–15 minutes in second stage.
safetyTips: Never leave a Category II or III strip unaddressed — escalate promptly.
Late decelerations (starting after peak of contraction) suggest uteroplacental insufficiency — report immediately.
Variable decelerations (abrupt onset/offset) suggest cord compression — reposition to relieve.
keyTakeaways: Moderate variability (6–25 bpm) is the most reassuring sign

title: Postpartum Uterine & BUBBLE-HE Assessment
summary: Systematic postpartum assessment using the BUBBLE-HE framework: Breasts, Uterus, Bowel, Bladder, Lochia, Episiotomy/incision, Homan's, Emotions.
steps: Perform hand hygiene. Explain assessment to patient. Ensure privacy.
B — Breasts: Inspect for engorgement, cracking, mastitis signs. Assess for colostrum/milk let-down if breastfeeding.
U — Uterus: Palpate fundus. Normal: firm, midline, at or below umbilicus (descends 1 cm/day). If boggy — perform fundal massage.
FUNDAL MASSAGE: Cup the lower uterine segment with non-dominant hand. Gently massage the fundus with the other until firm.
B — Bowel: Assess for return of bowel sounds. Ask about flatus, first BM. Encourage early ambulation.
B — Bladder: Palpate for distension. Encourage void q2–4h. Urine output >30mL/hr expected.
L — Lochia: Assess color (rubra → serosa → alba), amount (scant/light/moderate/heavy), and odor. Report foul-smelling or heavy (soaking pad in 15 min).
E — Episiotomy/Incision: Inspect for REEDA (Redness, Edema, Ecchymosis, Discharge, Approximation). Apply ice pack for first 24h.
H — Homan's Sign (limited utility): Assess for calf tenderness, warmth, redness (DVT risk is elevated postpartum).
E — Emotions: Screen for postpartum depression/anxiety using Edinburgh scale. Assess bonding and support system.
Document all findings and compare to prior assessment.
safetyTips: A boggy, displaced uterus = likely full bladder — have patient void first before attributing to uterine atony.
Heavy lochia + hypotension + tachycardia = postpartum hemorrhage — activate emergency response.
Edinburgh score ≥10 warrants provider notification and follow-up.
keyTakeaways: Fundus should firm up with massage
Postpartum hemorrhage is the leading cause of maternal mortality

title: Newborn Assessment & APGAR Scoring
summary: Assessing the newborn immediately after birth using APGAR and performing the initial head-to-toe neonatal assessment.
steps: Dry and stimulate newborn immediately upon delivery. Place under radiant warmer.
Suction mouth then nose (only if needed — routine suctioning not recommended).
APGAR at 1 minute and 5 minutes (and 10 min if score <7):
A — Appearance (skin color): 0=blue all over, 1=blue extremities, 2=pink all over
P — Pulse: 0=absent, 1=<100, 2=≥100
G — Grimace (reflex irritability): 0=none, 1=grimace, 2=cry/cough/sneeze
A — Activity (muscle tone): 0=limp, 1=some flexion, 2=active motion
R — Respiration: 0=absent, 1=weak cry, 2=strong cry
Score 7–10 = normal. Score 4–6 = moderate depression (stimulate, O2). Score 0–3 = severe (initiate resuscitation).
Apply ID bands to infant and mother before leaving delivery room.

Initial newborn assessment: head circumference, length, weight. Assess fontanels, eyes, palate, clavicles, umbilical cord (2 arteries, 1 vein), digits, hips (Ortolani/Barlow), reflexes (Moro, rooting, grasp).
First bath after temperature stabilizes (axillary ≥36.5°C / 97.7°F).
Administer erythromycin eye ointment and vitamin K IM per orders/protocol.
safetyTips: Delay cord clamping 30–60 seconds unless resuscitation is required.
Hypothermia is the #1 preventable cause of neonatal morbidity — keep warm.
APGAR does not predict long-term outcomes — it guides immediate resuscitation decisions.
documentation: Time of first breath, first cry
keyTakeaways: Dry, stimulate, warm are the first three interventions

title: Epidural Analgesia Monitoring & Management
summary: Monitoring and managing epidural analgesia in laboring patients, including assessment of sensory/motor block and complications.
equipment: Emergency medications: ephedrine, epinephrine, naloxone, intralipid emulsion at bedside
steps: Ensure IV access is patent and NS bolus (500–1000mL) given prior to epidural placement (per anesthesia orders).
After placement: monitor BP every 5 minutes × 20 minutes, then per facility policy (hypotension is the most common complication).
Assess sensory block level using ice or cold sensation — report levels above T6 to anesthesia.
Assess motor block: ask patient to move legs. Bromage scale: 0=full movement, 3=no movement. Report dense motor block to anesthesia.
Position patient: lateral or wedge under right hip — avoid aorta/vena cava compression.
Monitor FHR continuously — epidural can cause maternal hypotension → uteroplacental insufficiency.
Assess for: itching (opioid side effect — treat with naloxone or diphenhydramine), urinary retention, nausea.
Do NOT give IV opioids without anesthesia approval — additive CNS/respiratory depression risk.
High spinal emergency: sudden inability to speak, breathlessness, BP crash — call anesthesia STAT, lay flat, O2, vasopressors.
Document all assessments per policy. Inspect catheter site each shift for infection or migration.
safetyTips: Hypotension (<90 mmHg systolic or 20% drop from baseline): lateral position, IV fluid bolus, notify anesthesia, ephedrine per order.
Pruritus is common with intrathecal opioids — not an allergy.
Never inject anything into the epidural catheter without anesthesia order — wrong-route errors are fatal.
documentation: BP and HR q5 min × 20 min post-bolus
keyTakeaways: Hypotension is the most common complication

title: Oxytocin (Pitocin) Infusion Management
summary: Titrating IV oxytocin for labor induction or augmentation and monitoring for uterine tachysystole.
equipment: Oxytocin solution per order (typically 10–20 units in 500mL–1L NS)
steps: Obtain provider order including starting dose (typically 0.5–2 mU/min) and titration instructions.
Prepare oxytocin solution per pharmacy or order. Use infusion pump — never free-flow.
Initiate EFM before starting oxytocin.
Start infusion at prescribed rate. Titrate per order (typically increase by 1–2 mU/min every 15–40 min).
Assess uterine activity: goal is contractions every 2–3 minutes, lasting 60–90 seconds, with adequate rest between.
TACHYSYSTOLE = >5 contractions in 10 minutes: STOP or decrease oxytocin, reposition, increase IV fluids, apply O2, notify provider.
Monitor: maternal BP, HR, urine output (oxytocin has antidiuretic effect — watch for water intoxication with high doses).
Continuously monitor FHR — look for late decelerations (uteroplacental compromise).
Titrate down once labor well established; may discontinue when active phase maintained.
NEVER give IV oxytocin bolus — must be infused on a pump.
safetyTips: Oxytocin is a HIGH-ALERT medication — independent double-check required for dose and pump settings.
Tachysystole with non-reassuring FHR = emergency — stop infusion and notify provider immediately.
Prolonged high-dose oxytocin + excess free water = hyponatremia/water intoxication.

title: Breastfeeding Support & Latch Assessment
summary: Assessing and supporting breastfeeding initiation, latch, and maternal confidence in the postpartum period.
steps: Encourage breastfeeding within the first hour after birth (skin-to-skin).
Assess readiness cues: rooting, sucking on hands, alertness.
Help mother achieve proper position: cradle, cross-cradle, football, or side-lying.
Instruct on proper latch: infant mouth wide open, lower lip flanged out, chin touching breast, nose clear. Most of the areola should be in the mouth (not just the nipple).
LATCH Score: L=Latch, A=Audible swallowing, T=Type of nipple, C=Comfort, H=Hold (0–10; higher = better).
Assess milk transfer: listen for audible swallows, assess infant satisfaction after feeding, monitor infant weight.
Feeding frequency: 8–12 times per 24 hours (on demand). Each breast ~10–20 minutes.
Assess for engorgement: encourage frequent feeding, warm compresses before feeding, cold compresses after.
Mastitis signs: localized warmth, redness, fever >38.5°C — continue breastfeeding, refer to provider for antibiotics if needed.
Document LATCH score, feeding duration, infant behavior post-feed.
safetyTips: Nipple pain is NOT normal after the first days — reassess latch.
Jaundice can worsen with inadequate intake — monitor bilirubin and feeding frequency.
Inverted nipples may require a nipple shield — refer to lactation consultant.
documentation: Referral to lactation consultant if needed
